stories.headline: 'Mixed Metaphors': A monster, a bridge, or a phantom?
stories.deck: A monster, a bridge, or a phantom?
stories.bodyText: Mother is the most overused metaphor of all time. Daisy Rockwell’s treatise on the (mis)adventures of translation opens with the same image, stirred up for better reasons. This is a poem by Mary Ruefle, who valorises mothers as the first translators in the history of mankind — ‘a mother heard her baby babble or cry, and had to decide in an instant what it meant’. Against such maternal holiness, Daisy rips open the image from end to end, with great wit, describing what a literary translator does in a day if she happens to be a mother indeed. These are images of unromantic labour: tending to a screaming child while staring at books for hours, or sitting in the waiting room of a dance studio writing out her translations in a small notebook, perched on a folding metal chair. Surrounded by bells and whistles as she translates a Hindi bildungsroman into English... recurring interruptions that unite her with her author, also a woman, who is trying hard to write..This is a new metaphor, somewhat mixed and certainly fleshier, that refuses the age-old conception of translation as child-bearing, and returns women translators to their real seats, in front of difficult sentences..A humorous assemblage of poems, notes, and gossip, Mixed Metaphors is a reminder that there is tinkering and art in translation despite its overrated ‘losses’. While there are no easy recipes for the Booker Prize here, this book holds another rare assurance: that anxious, depressed young translators who are still finding their way and being disillusioned by ruthless publishers might want to hold on to their work, and see it as art in its own right. Her form and candour are more evidence that these translators will grow up to be funny, thrilling writers..Not just a transfer of words.Translation is a bridge, a phantom, a Lego set, a wedding, even a monster. The metaphor is used as an inventive form that can capture the different relationships at play in literary translation — between author and translator, between the translator and their creation, and sometimes even to comment on the publishing world — without reducing them to formulae or lessons..Most of these images cement what the work of re-making might be, and imagine it as more than a mechanical transfer of words from one dictionary to another. Translation is monstrous like Frankenstein, greeted with screams by purists, but exciting wonderment in its maker. Like a paper replica of a beautiful quilt, it doesn’t serve the same function as the original, but still keeps one of its qualities, in this case, beauty..The most striking metaphors here situate the role of translation in epistemic violence. ‘English is the potato crop for McDonald’s french fries’, a note explains, and its far reach and continuing dominance is evidence of empire and extraction, not just by colonial powers but also capitalism..In another poem, a djinn is packed in a bottle and carried across oceans by the translator, but when it reaches the shores of the West, it becomes a ‘Genie’, a fetishised Oriental object that is feared and ridiculed. Rockwell writes from within this empire and shows how translation, as a site of language, makes it possible to understand the inequities between English and many non-Englishes..Then there are copyright tales, spanning from her time as a young translator to the now-famed doyenne of the field. If there is one thing that has changed very little, it is how hair-raising these tales are. In these stories, the personalities of Hindi-Urdu authors come across as moody, particular, and thrilling. These literary biopics highlight something sharp about writing itself, but more than that, they are a ‘pardafash’, exposing what surrounds the act of writing: opportunist sons, unpublished books, parasitic publishers, and a publishing ecosystem that doesn’t give bhasha writers (and their translators) the due respect they deserve..The most tender, by far, is the account of those who taught her translation. A K Ramanujan’s words, which Rockwell learnt as his student in Chicago, ring in the ears of many translators of South Asia who have followed in his footsteps. The book retraces him in a very Hindi-Urdu reverence, calling him ‘they’, perhaps an apt translation of ‘aap’..The many exciting illustrations in the book truly capture what Mixed Metaphors is. A rare patchwork on language and literature, for those who despise boring lectures and prefer eclectic, honest teachers.

stories.headline: Sowing the seeds of a solar power intervention
stories.deck: India’s emerging agrivoltaics model enables farmers to grow crops beneath solar panels, offering a way to generate electricity while diversifying income. Vanita Bhatnagar speaks to farmers and agri-researchers to find out how high upfront costs, financing constraints, and uneven policy support are preventing more farmers from taking up projects beyond the pilots
stories.bodyText:
Kojadmal Jat’s solar farm is different from those surrounding it. In Kundanpura, a village in Bassi block, nearly an hour’s drive east of Jaipur, Rajasthan’s capital, the sight of fields dotted with rows of ground-mounted solar panels is now common. On 60-year-old Jat’s land, though, tender maize unfurls under the dark glass of the panels reflecting the afternoon light. The maize, in shades of pale yellow and green, fills a space that conventional solar farms leave barren.
Jat has been working with researchers of Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations (ICRIER) on an agrophotovoltaics (APV) project.
Also known as agrivoltaics or agriPV, this is a practice in which the same land is used for agriculture and solar power generation.
His farm is part of a pilot, spread across nearly 3 acres, roughly twice the size of a cricket ground. This is Rajasthan’s first farmer-owned APV, which generates 600 kW. The installation feeds enough electricity into a local grid to provide daytime irrigation power for around 250 farms.
In 2023, inspired by the growing solar-panel-covered fields of his neighbours, Jat exchanged the uncertainties of each harvest for the predictability of monthly income. His decision exposes a dilemma at the heart of the energy transition: should productive farmland generate food or electricity? Jat was anguished by this trade-off. “My farm was generating solar power, but at the end of the day, I am a farmer. I could not come to terms with the fact that I was no longer able to cultivate my land because of the solar panels.”
India ranks 102nd out of 123 countries, on the 2025 Global Hunger Index. Converting productive farmlands to solar power plants risks intensifying food insecurity.
APV works on the principle that partial shading from solar panels can reduce heat stress and evaporation while creating a more stable microclimate, potentially valuable for farming in dry and arid regions. Laxmi Sharma, a research associate with the ICRIER team, was assigned the job of helping Jat explore the APV model. “When we showed him that he could combine farming with solar energy generation, he was delighted by the prospect of being able to do both,” she recalls.
By diversifying farm income, the model reduces dependence on a single source of livelihood and strengthens resilience to both climatic and market risks. But the economics that make APV attractive also constrain its wider adoption. APV can increase farmers’ annual returns of roughly ₹3 lakh to ₹4 lakh per acre, but elevated mounting structures add nearly ₹35 lakh over a conventional installation. For many smallholder farmers, this is simply out of reach
Farmers as solar entrepreneurs
Jat had spent a lifetime farming before turning to solar energy. Through farming he was able to earn close to ₹40,000 a year, but with these panels, his annual income has increased nearly eightfold, to about ₹3 lakh.
In mid-2024, a young team of researchers in New Delhi set out to study the viability of a farmer-owned agrivoltaics model. “When we started, there were only around two dozen agrivoltaics pilots in India,” says Sharma, who joined ICRIER in 2024 for this project. “Most were led by academic institutions or private developers and very few were actually owned by farmers.”
In Madhya Pradesh, Anand Jain, an MTech graduate from IIT Roorkee and a farmer since the 1990s, had arrived at the same question from a different direction. He started studying agrivoltaic projects in Germany and other parts of Europe, collecting data on panel height, spacing, and the microclimate created beneath them.
“Because I am a farmer, I wanted to save every inch of my land,” he says. The panels, he reasoned, should adapt to the farm, not force the farm out.
His own experiment became an early example of the kind of farmer-led model that ICRIER would later seek to study more systematically.
The ICRIER team distilled its findings in an April 2025 report titled ‘Solar as a Third Crop to Augment Farmers’ Income’. They then set out to test this idea in the field.
Rajasthan was their natural choice because the State has India’s highest solar irradiation. It was among the leading implementers of the PM-KUSUM, a Central government scheme, which offers incentives to farmers using solar energy. The ICRIER team partnered with a grassroots organisation to find a farmer willing to test the model. Their search led them to Jat.
Taking the risk
Jat and his family were intrigued but cautious. “My first question was about trust,” he says. “We are often shown ambitious schemes and glossy promises, but when things go south, we are left to navigate the uncertainty and financial risk on our own,” recalls Shiv, 36, Jat’s son, who was closely involved with his father in the APV project.
The researchers, meanwhile, had their own doubts. They wanted to know whether Jat was serious enough about farming to continue cultivating the land for the next 25 years. “For us, Kojadmal was a stranger. For Kojadmal, we were just another group of experts. Trust had to be built through multiple conversations,” recalls Laxmi.
Jat and his son say that their experience with ICRIER’s earlier work made the difference. The team had already been working with farmers on a net-house project, and they had seen their efforts first-hand. “They didn’t just come and tell us about a plan, they were there, working with us and showing us what they were doing. I had seen their team’s hard work on the ground. That is what earned our trust,” says Shiv.
They worked through the technical and financial details together, but Jat knew that the final risk would still be his. “This wasn’t free money,” says Subhodeep Basu, a researcher at ICRIER, who worked on the ‘Solar as a Third Crop…’ study. If agrivoltaics were to create farmer-entrepreneurs rather than grant recipients, Jat had to invest in the project himself and share its risks.
Trusting the process
The next challenge lay in retrofitting an operational solar plant. “A lot of individual farmers told us, ‘We already have a steady source of income. If construction means losing energy revenue during that period, we’re not interested,’” recalls Subhodeep. Hence, instead of shutting down the entire plant, they retrofitted it, one inverter at a time, allowing the remaining sections to continue generating electricity. “That way we could minimise this energy loss,” says Subhodeep.
The ICRIER team decided to advise farmers on which crops were most likely to thrive beneath the panels, while leaving the final choice to them. They would shoulder the risk and reap the returns. Jat chose maize, hoping to grow it during the off season under the cooler microclimate created by the panels, when supplies were thin and prices higher. “In May, the heat made planting impossible but this year, we harvested an abundant maize crop with much less water. The panels have made it possible to farm where it was once impossible,” says Shiv.
With the engineering finalised and the crop chosen, the last question was whether the economics could make the model viable. Like the conventional solar project, 70% of the upfront cost would come from a commercial bank loan carrying an interest rate of 10.25%. For this pilot, the additional cost of retrofitting, i.e., ₹35.3 lakh, was provided by Kotak Mahindra through their CSR programme Kotak Karma.
The electricity generated by the plant would continue to flow into the grid, where Rajasthan’s distribution utility, Jaipur Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. (JVVNL), would purchase it at ₹3.14 per unit for 25 years. The plant would generate electricity every day of the year. “To understand the financial feasibility of the pilot, we modelled two scenarios, one with viability gap funding (VGF, a government scheme) and another without it,” adds Subhodeep. Without VGF, Jat would have had to wait nearly 12 years to recover his investment. With VGF covering part of the upfront cost, that wait was cut almost in half, to just over six years. The project also became substantially more rewarding as annual profits increased from ₹3.76 lakh to ₹4.48 lakh per acre, while the expected return on investment rose from 12% to 18%.
Between promise and scale
GIZ India, a German development agency that funded the project, found that 54% of the 1,700 farmers it engaged through workshops expressed interest in adopting agriPV systems.
Another farmer who had watched Jat’s project evolve from its earliest days admitted he had often imagined replicating it on his own land. “Kojadmal could take the risk,” he says. “I’d like to as well. I already have a ground-mounted solar plant. But I don’t have the appetite to take such a big loan or put in that kind of money.”
High capital costs continue to deter participation, says Ashok Gulati, an agricultural economist and professor at ICRIER. With lending rates hovering around 10.5%, the economics remain challenging for most farmers, he adds.
“Many state distribution companies remain reluctant to sign long-term power-purchase agreements because of financial stress or surplus power. Land approvals, bureaucratic delays and shifting policy guidelines have slowed implementation,” explains Gulati.
He also suggests that a credit guarantee backed by the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) could make smaller agriPV projects easier to finance. But for now, no such financing window exists, a NABARD official confirmed. What does exist is a carefully structured repayment system that gives banks confidence to lend.
Jain sees the implementation gap from the ground. PM-KUSUM is a Central scheme, but execution is entirely at the State level. “There should be a single-window system under the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE), so farmers are not left navigating this maze on their own.”
He took more than nine months to get the power-purchase agreement done. Meters added another hidden cost: at around ₹5 lakh each, four meters meant ₹20 lakh before the plant could even begin generating returns. “How is this feasible for an ordinary farmer?” he asks.
Further, the paperwork carries a steep price: stamp duty on registered mortgage agreements for solar projects can run into lakhs of rupees, adding another upfront cost to an already capital-intensive investment.
Rajasthan’s energy department, however, says the process has been streamlined, with nodal officers, standardised procedures, simpler land acquisition processes and the shifting of implementation from the Rajasthan Renewable Energy Corporation to power distribution companies. The State now has over 3,000 MW of installed solar capacity and daytime power reaching farmers across at least 22 districts. But that ease is not uniform across States. In Madhya Pradesh, Jain had to deal with three separate energy departments.
Even in Rajasthan, agriPV has no dedicated procurement pathway and must compete with conventional ground-mounted solar in tenders designed around lower-cost PV, despite its higher capital costs and added agricultural benefits.
The price of possibility
Financing is only one constraint. A senior NABARD official, speaking anonymously, says weak rural-grid capacity and concerns about absorbing decentralised solar power have made NABARD cautious about dedicated agriPV financing.
Rajasthan sanctions PM-KUSUM plants only where substations have capacity and is planning large-scale battery energy storage systems to absorb surplus daytime generation, though storage adds capital costs.
While PM-KUSUM has been in operation since 2019, there is no centralised monitoring or grievance redressal cell.
Gulati argues that the next phase of PM-KUSUM must strengthen the ecosystem that supports farmers by identifying crop varieties and establishing a centralised agriPV monitoring portal under MNRE to track project commissioning, power exports, and payment timelines. It must also create a single platform for grievance redressal and coordination among DISCOMs, state nodal agencies and implementation partners.
Shirish Garud, now a consultant with The Energy and Resources Institute and a former senior fellow and director, argues that India needs a dedicated Renewable Purchase Obligation for agrivoltaics.
While the Electricity Act, 2003, already requires distribution companies to procure a fixed share of their electricity from renewable sources, the mandate makes no distinction between conventional solar and agriPV.
Subrahmanyam Pulipaka, CEO, National Solar Energy Federation of India, says that for agriPV to move beyond pilots, India must first establish a clear definition of what constitutes an agriPV project. Unlike countries such as Germany, France and Japan, which have clear standards governing agrivoltaics, India does not yet have formal standards, technical benchmarks, or eligibility criteria.
The next priority is to build a robust evidence base. “We should now scale it across all agro-climatic regions and generate reliable data on agricultural productivity, solar generation, and project economics,” Pulipaka says.
Krishi Vigyan Kendras and agricultural universities, he says, should lead these demonstrations by training farmers in identifying locally suitable cropping patterns and building confidence in the technology.
Pulipaka says farmer-producer organisations and cooperatives are fundamental to this capital-intensive, knowledge-intensive model. “FPOs can aggregate farmers, build awareness, provide technical support, and make project implementation more efficient,” he adds.

stories.headline: ICG deploys ships for search-and-rescue operation after Panama-flagged vessel sinks
stories.deck: The ship, with 24 crew members on board, was heading towards Singapore carrying iron ore from Odisha
stories.bodyText:
The Indian Coast Guard (ICG) has deployed three of its ships for a search-and-rescue operation after a Panama-flagged bulk carrier, carrying 24 crew members, sank in the Bay of Bengal, about 240 nautical miles from the Paradip coast of Odisha, on Saturday (August 22, 2026), officials said.
The bulk carrier, M.V. Ocean Winner, was carrying “20 Chinese, three Myanmarese and one Bangladeshi” on board, an ICG spokesperson said.
The vessel’s last port of call was Paradip and next port of call was Singapore, the official added.
ICG’s Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre (MRCC) in Sri Vijaya Puram received an information from a company associated with the vessel “at 1148 hrs regarding loss of communication with MV Ocean Winner (IMO 9145530), with 24 crew onboard, and a request for search and rescue assistance”, the ICG spokesperson said.
The ship was carrying iron ore from Odisha, officials had earlier said. The ICG and the Indian Navy have launched the rescue operation, they said.
The MRCC diverted MT Aisopos, a commercial vessel which was in the vicinity, to “search for the vessel or liferafts and render assistance, and the vessel recovered two survivors from two liferafts at about 2000 hrs”, the ICG spokesperson added.
ICG ships “Varad” and “Anmol” have been deployed for the search-and-rescue efforts, while “Vijit” has also been deployed from Sri Vijaya Puram to augment the operation, the official added.

stories.headline: Trump shares image calling Hormuz 'new US territory'; Iran says strait 'closed'
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: US President Donald Trump on Sunday again shared an image on Truth Social describing the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz as “NEW US Territory”, even as Iran maintained that the waterway was closed and would remain so unless Washington changed its approach.
Trump had first shared the same image on August 18. Speaking at a police academy on Long Island on August 14, he had said, “Pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Strait of Hormuz a territory of the United States.”
Iran’s supreme national security council secretary Mohsen Rezaei, meanwhile, said Tehran would not reopen the strait unless the US fulfilled its commitments and changed its behaviour.
“The Strait of Hormuz is closed and will not reopen,” Iran International quoted Rezaei saying. “If the United States changes its behavior and fulfills its commitments, the equation will be different, but this time the United States must act. It cannot be resolved through words and talks.”
Despite Iran’s declaration, traffic through the waterway has increased in recent days. Nearly 200 ships crossed the Hormuz last week, compared with about 150 the previous week and around 40 two weeks earlier, according to UK maritime trade operations data cited by the New York Post.
Maritime intelligence firm Kpler said more than 80% of liquid cargoes passing through the strait over the past two weeks either used an Omani route backed by the US and authorised by the International Maritime Organization, or went “dark”.
Rezaei also said Iran had reached an agreement with Oman on a “middle route” through the strait, although a joint statement had yet to be finalised.

briefs.headline: 'Aurangzeb Alamgir': Minus myths, an emperor
briefs.deck: Minus myths, an emperor
briefs.bodyText: Aurangzeb has been dead for nearly 319 years, and he has rarely been busier. No other early modern ruler anywhere is litigated with such heat by people who could not even date his reign to the correct half-century..Into this heat comes Munis D Faruqui’s biography of Aurangzeb, 30 years in the making, begun in graduate-school conversations with the late John F Richards in 1995, and built on a proposition so mild it amounts to provocation: that the sixth Mughal emperor was, in many ways that mattered, an ordinary king..Writing a figure as contested as Aurangzeb as typical or ordinary is to make him more complicated. Faruqui’s work shows how complications, and not caricatures, made the Mughal Empire reach its extent under his hand and begin to decline in his lifetime..Faruqui, by his own account, viewed the emperor as a “religious bigot,” and was moved to write only by a “growing horror at the falsifying and weaponising” of Mughal history in contemporary India. What follows is a scholar arguing against his earlier instincts, while being fully aware of the polemics his book will land in, staying prepared to resist them..Yash Saxena’s 'Stories from a Kargili Kitchen'| A glimpse of Kargil, beyond war tropes.Even the name on the page and typography — Aurangzeb until 1658, and ‘Alamgir thereafter — restores the regnal title that historian Jadunath Sarkar’s five volumes (1912–24) set aside..Banking on imperial bulletins.The spine of the book is an archive that previous biographers have barely touched — the akhbarat-i darbar-i mu’alla, thousands of daily news bulletins of the imperial court that let a historian watch a government functioning rather than being commemorated. From them, Faruqui reconstructs a court in granular motion. Aurangzeb rises as an emperor who read everything, trusted few, and governed as much through pen and informant as through the sword..The book is not a defence of the emperor, and the author has no qualms calling his subject “a failed imperialist” whose Deccan wars “ultimately collapsed” the empire..Three arguments recur through the book. Faruqui has no patience with Sarkar’s picture of an undeserving “freak of Fortune.” The throne was won by “decades-long efforts” of network-building, consolidation and reputation-making, and in the “dog-eat-dog world” of Mughal politics after the 1580s, “Aurangzeb’s actions were unexceptional.” Faruqui contends that in a world where every prince played that game, this one played it best..Second, Alamgir depended “heavily, and significantly more than previous emperors” on the imperial harem and the eunuchs of the household..Third, the reign is “most usefully and accurately understood as transitional,” with the hinge falling in 1690 rather than the canonical 1658 or 1707..What the chronicles don’t say.The second yields the most genuinely new history. Two chapters reveal what the chronicles never show: Zinat al-Nisa, the emperor’s daughter, who ran the inner treasury and reconciled feuding princes, arguably the second power in the empire by its end; and the eunuch Khidmatgar Khan III, who managed the court through the 1690s. That they stayed invisible for three centuries says something about what the chronicles chose to record..Then came the Deccan. The emperor crushed his rebel son Akbar, and the Maratha state Shivaji had built in 1681, and followed it up with annexures and the capture and execution of Shivaji’s son Sambhaji. He then spent 18 years besieging hill forts that were retaken behind him, while the northern administration decayed from inattention. While this has been explained by historian Athar Ali, Faruqui adds what the correspondence makes credible — that the Deccan had become a matter of personal honour and religious duty for the ageing emperor..The last years form the most haunting pages — Aurangzeb is sketched as an 88-year-old sovereign, half-blind, nominally the richest man on earth, ignored by his commanders, spied on by his sons, writing that God had abandoned him..Historian and author William Dalrymple has called the book “a study in profound failure,” and these pages show why. Whether the inner life of a 17th-century emperor can really be read from his letters is a fair question; the letters were performances too, composed in a well-worn idiom of pious self-abasement, and Faruqui might have said so more insistently than he does..Colonial portrayal.Faruqi argues that Aurangzeb’s negative reputation today is largely a product of late 18th- and 19th-century colonial historiography, rather than a continuation of how he was remembered by his contemporaries. In the decades immediately after his death, Aurangzeb had been commemorated as a capable administrator and indefatigable warrior, with admiration extending beyond the Mughal court. It was only under colonial influence that this positive memory was recast. Colonial historians increasingly portrayed Aurangzeb as a religiously intolerant, fanatical, and failed emperor while elevating Akbar as the ideal king..Faruqui contends that this shift selectively privileged sectarian and polemical accounts while overlooking the 18th-century nuanced corpus that emphasised Aurangzeb’s strengths..This is the first full scholarly life of Alamgir in a century, and it does what such a book should: not end the quarrel, but raise the price of entering it uninformed. Sarkar held the field for a century: He has, at last, a successor worth disagreeing with.

briefs.headline: The garden where no one kept count
briefs.deck: The garden where no one kept count
briefs.bodyText: As the years pass, I realise that the India of my childhood is disappearing — not only from maps and institutions, but from living memory. More than 70 years have passed since I last saw Imphal through the eyes of a five-year-old, yet I can still walk through that world without a map. Time has faded many things, but not those afternoons after the monsoon..The rain would stop as suddenly as it had begun, leaving the garden washed clean and glistening. My mother would be resting after lunch. To a five-year-old, that was the signal that the afternoon belonged to adventure. The garden was my kingdom and its caretakers were my companions..Beyond the garden flowed a river. On the opposite bank stood a small hill. During the monsoon it swelled into a muddy torrent. In winter it became gentler, revealing smooth stones along the banks. To me, however, it remained simply the forbidden river. Naturally, this made it irresistible. I would creep up to the bund, listening to frogs croak after the rain and poking leeches with a stick as they inched across the wet earth..My first stop in the garden was the jamun tree. The ground beneath it would be carpeted with half-eaten fruit — the unmistakable evidence of the bats’ night shift. Uma, who looked after odd jobs in the garden and pumped water into the overhead tank, would promptly steer me away from the fallen berries towards the guava tree. Every few weeks he fashioned a catapult for me from a guava branch..Only years later did I suspect that the catapult was only half the reason. The other half was the opportunity to exchange a few words with Eichi, who tended the tulsi plant with quiet devotion, softly chanting her prayers. From there I wandered among the mango trees and flower beds overflowing with sweet peas, phlox, gladioli, sunflowers and, when evening approached, the unforgettable fragrance of the Queen of the Night..Near the driveway stood Adom, always ready to take me for a slow ride in his car or patiently steady my bicycle while I struggled to master the mysteries of balance. Soon Taipi, my sister’s nanny, would call me home for tea and freshly baked scones. In her spare moments, she sat patiently at a loom that my mother had arranged for her, weaving shawls with a concentration that fascinated me. More than 70 years later, I still have one of them..After tea, I would make my way to the veranda where Bishambher and Moiuddinbhai, my father’s office attendants, sat knitting socks with long wooden needles — a skill that has defeated me throughout my life. As the needles clicked rhythmically, they filled my afternoons with stories. They spoke of old Manipur, of kings, warriors, temples and traditions that stretched back centuries. I understood little of what they said, but I remember that whenever their conversations turned to the merger of Manipur with India, their voices became quieter. Even as a child, I sensed that they were speaking not merely of history but of something deeply personal. Only decades later did I understand why. It never occurred to me then that the people who shaped my childhood belonged to different communities. Uma, Eichi and Bishambher were Meitei. Adom and Taipi were Kuki. I never knew Moiuddinbhai’ s ancestry, nor did it matter to me. They were simply my friends..That may be the most remarkable memory of all. The adults around me knew perfectly well who belonged to which community. Yet they worked together, laughed together, teased one another and, without ever setting out to do so, taught a little girl that people came before identities. The Imphal I carry in my memory and the Manipur of today’s headlines are separated by far more than the passage of time..Somewhere along the way, something infinitely precious began to fray. Peace between communities is seldom accidental. It grows slowly through fairness, trust and the quiet confidence that every family belongs. When those foundations weaken, familiarity gives way to suspicion, and identities begin to overshadow friendships..But even so, whenever I think of Manipur, I do not begin with conflict. I begin with a rain-soaked garden.

briefs.headline: Of life and hope unbound
briefs.deck: Of life and hope unbound
briefs.bodyText: For a word that seems to be strict about defining the perimeter of individual spaces, it’s surprising that the word ‘bound’ should have a life so predicated on the prefix and suffix. In osmotic linguistic cultures like ours, the first time we encounter the word in some form is perhaps in the phrase ‘boundary wall’. It conditions us to map our own bodies, the skin, and then toes and skull, the equivalents of country and continent. When we go to the origin of the word, there’s a surprise – that it came from seemingly opposite directions, bringing together, tying, as in ‘bound’ and ‘binding’, as well as the circumscribing of space, as, say, we find in the way it’s used to characterise a box-like wall inside which sits a cake-like building..‘Bound’ and ‘bouquet’ share the first three letters. In both, there is tying, collecting, or gathering, whether it’s flowers from neighbouring habitats or pages in what is about to become a book. These flowers or pages could be identical to each other, but that is not usually the case – different paragraphs, different kinds of flowers, what is being brought together is not a family (tree) but an ad hoc arrangement, a semi-permanent companionship between different species, whether it be flowers or thoughts. That they were often understood to be genetically similar is made evident in a semi-stock phrase such as ‘a bouquet of songs and sonnets’ or ‘a bouquet of poems’. A phrase like that would provide the title for poetry collections and anthologies for many generations. That it should be composed of multiple things not necessarily related to each other was inherent in the history of ‘bouquet’ itself. Originally meaning a ‘grove of trees’, it soon became lenient, coming to stand for a ‘cluster’ of trees. I say ‘lenient’, but what I probably mean is an elastic accommodativeness..Limits of the colonised mind.How then could such a word, that glued disparate things, also come to mean something that kept things out, as in the ‘boundary’ wall? To understand this is to become aware of one’s jaw tightening at the bristly relationship between the outside and inside. The rules inside the ‘boundary wall’ of one’s house – or ‘compound’ – are different from those outside it. The boundary creates restrictions, physical but, more importantly, psychological. Of the kind, say, I feel when writing this ‘column’ – a closed space with well-marked boundaries created by editors and the design team. There’s the word ‘limit’, so that what I say does not spill out of the boundary wall of this column. I am bound by that contract with the editor even as I write from what I might understand as an unbounded spirit..Why did Shelley feel so emotionally and creatively driven to free Prometheus from Prometheus Bound? Aeschylus had written a trilogy, and Prometheus Unbound had been one of them, but only Prometheus Bound was extant; the other two were lost to history. I’m tempted to see this loss as defining Western civilisation the way the loss of Aristotle’s theory of comedy has – the first censoring audacity of the creative spirit, the second turning the tragic as Western man’s default residency. Prometheus had, as we know, stolen fire for humans, to whom he had also given the arts and sciences – music as much as medicine and metalwork, writing and numbers – for which he’d been punished by Zeus. In Aeschylus’s lost play, there is ‘reconciliation of Jupiter with his victim’, as Shelley put it, and it was this mild reconciliation that the Romantic poet wanted to challenge..‘I was averse from a catastrophe so feeble as that of reconciling the Champion with the Oppressor of mankind. The moral interest of the fable, which is so powerfully sustained by the sufferings and endurance of Prometheus, would be annihilated if we could conceive of him as unsaying his high language and quailing before his successful and perfidious adversary,’ he wrote in the introduction to his ‘lyrical drama’, a play that was meant more for the ear and the mind than the stage..What does being unbound mean? ‘To defy power, which seems omnipotent;/ To love, and bear; to hope till Hope creates/ From its own wreck the thing it contemplates;/...Good, great and joyous, beautiful and free;/ This is alone Life, Joy, Empire, and Victory.’ This is a manifesto that the French Revolution – under whose spell Shelley wrote his Prometheus – made possible. I’ve found myself returning to these lines lately, thinking of an India Unbound..The writer is an author and poet. Her books include How I Became a Tree and Provincials.Disclaimer: The views expressed above are the author's own. briefs.headline: Limits of the colonised mind
briefs.deck: Limits of the colonised mind
briefs.bodyText: In his Discourse on Colonialism, which first appeared in 1950, Aimé Césaire examines the psychological, sociological, and pseudo-civilisational underpinnings of the colonialist enterprise, whether in Africa, Latin America, or Asia. He exposes the hypocrisy and contradictions implicit in Western notions of ‘progress’ and ‘civilisation’ upon encountering the ‘savage’, the ‘primitive’, and the ‘uncultured’—terms solely reserved for describing and denigrating non-Western, non-Christian societies. Western adventurers, with no moral or ethical compass but proudly professing to be Christian, went to great lengths to acquire the territories and resources of non-white populations and evangelise them..Césaire’s insightful remark, ‘It is [equally] necessary to decolonise our minds, our inner life, at the same time we decolonise society’ is applicable, even more so today than in the previous three centuries, simply because the overlords of technology in Silicon Valley have completely colonised our minds without our being aware of it and, in the process, become fabulously rich and situated themselves in a position to dictate the fate of individuals and nation-states alike. People like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, having colonised our hearts and minds, are looking for fresh territories to conquer, in outer space and the unfathomed depths of the oceans, before China gets there first. In Mao Zedong’s time, political power may have grown out of the barrel of a gun, but today, power comes from a string of bits and bytes..We have reached a point in society where face-to-face communication has been deliberately made impossible. Ordinary telephone communication between humans has been compromised through the introduction of automated voice agents at one end. In short, every act of human communication is now mediated by one digital artifice or another. If you recently purchased a product and are having problems with it, good luck getting a real, live human being at the company to intercede on your behalf. Automated agents cost little, but humans cost a lot..Some twenty years ago, there was great concern among the populace that it could no longer discern what was real and what was fake when viewing information on the web. With the advent of agentic AI such as ChatGPT and Gemini, we have reached a moment where anything we read, see or hear can be AI-generated. Attempting to distinguish between fake and deepfake is now an exercise in pitiful semantic quibbling, to be attempted only by the brave..We have all become so enamoured of AI that, in the process, we have closed our eyes to what is happening to our critical thinking skills. AI summaries have led us to avoid reading original documents in their entirety, even though the AI summary offered comes with a warning that what has been generated could contain errors. Ignoring the warning is akin to ignoring the fine print that accompanies every credit card application, investment opportunity or prescription/over-the-counter drug side effects. The onus is always on the customer, never the company offering the product. Caveat emptor..Slick advertising by Silicon Valley, whether on the web, smartphones or TV, has spread the FOMO (fear of missing out) syndrome, convincing the gullible that the latest AI-supplemented versions of their products are infinitely superior to whatever they currently own. The language of the coloniser has become the language of the colonised..Google has been successful in stealing millions of books without any credible legal challenges and making them available on the web. The multilingual translation services provided by Silicon Valley, while definitely useful, are in no way foolproof, as we can never know if the translation is correct or if something has been lost in translation. The gratuitous summaries offered by AI of all text may please the many amongst us who are lazy and uncritical, but not all. It is now possible to generate a person’s entire life story based solely on their online interactions with the world at large and post it on the web, an insidious practice known as doxxing, to the affected person’s dismay and detriment. Winning the user’s hearts and minds has never been easier since all we need are a few pointers for agentic AI to generate books, movies, theses, dissertations, op-ed pieces, biographies, and operas. To what end?.The leaning Tower of Pisa may still be standing when Silicon Valley’s Tower of Babel comes crashing down in a welter of confusion..The writer is a computer scientist, a newly minted Luddite and a cynic.Disclaimer: The views expressed above are the author's own. They do not necessarily reflect the views of DH..Write to us at: theprism@deccanherald.co.in

briefs.headline: Visit families affected by Ken-Betwa project, hear their grievances: M.P. CM tells officials
briefs.deck: Chief Minister Yadav directed the Panna and Chhatarpur district administrations to ensure that officials visit every household in the affected villages to understand the actual situation and problems of the families
briefs.bodyText:
Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister Mohan Yadav has directed officials to visit the villages in Panna and Chhatarpur districts and meet the families that are being impacted by the Ken Betwa river link project to hear their grievances.
Mr. Yadav issued the directions after holding a review meeting for the project in Khajuraho on Friday (August 21, 2026). The move comes just days after Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, met with a group of protestors who had staged demonstrations in April and July demanding better compensation and rehabilitation for the families affected by the Centre’s ₹44,000 crore Ken-Betwa Link Project [KBLP] as well as five M.P. Government works like the Majhgaon and Runjh irrigation projects.
Chief Minister Yadav directed the Panna and Chhatarpur district administrations to ensure that officials visit every household in the affected villages to understand the actual situation and problems of the families. He directed officials to listen sensitively to the difficulties faced by tribal families and resolve them on priority, a government statement said, after the review meeting.
Mr. Yadav also asked officials to ensure doorstep delivery of benefits of various government welfare schemes are reaching the eligible families that have been displaced due to the project.
“He said that where families have settled at new locations, concrete action plans should be prepared to provide essential facilities such as schools, Anganwadi centres, health centres and community halls,” the statement said.
In April and July, hundreds of tribals from villages in the two districts had staged ‘satyagrah’ protests in various forms, including by standing in water and lying on symbolic pyres on the banks of Barana river in Chhatarpur, against the
The demonstrations ended on July 19, after the Madhya Pradesh Police dismantled the protest site and forcibly admitted activist Amit Bhatnagar, who had been on a hunger strike, to a hospital.
Mr. Yadav also instructed officials to ensure early payment of the approved additional amount to those affected by the Runjh and Majhgaon projects in Panna.
The compensation for the two projects was increased from ₹5 lakh to ₹12.5 lakh for each affected family during the protests in July, bringing it on par with the compensation package of the KBLP.
Terming the KBLP a project of national importance, Mr. Yadav said that it would prove to be a milestone in the development of Bundelkhand region.
“The project would bring significant improvements in irrigation, drinking water supply and energy in the region. He said ensuring the welfare of affected and displaced families alongside development remains the government’s priority,” he said.
The project, kickstarted by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on December 25, 2024, aims to transfer excess water from the Ken river basin to the Betwa river basin in the region that covers parts of Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh. It is the first of 30 such link projects under a National Perspective Plan (NPP) for water resources development and interlinking of rivers with ‘surplus water’ to those with ‘deficit water’.
Earlier on August 19, Mr. Gandhi extended support to the affected villagers after meeting with Mr. Bhatnagar and other protestors, and said that he would visit the area.
“The problems, demands, struggles, and personal ordeals of the tribal brothers and sisters who are carrying out a satyagraha against the Ken-Betwa project—their own account. For years, these residents of Bundelkhand have been enduring injustice and oppression solely for their rights; they deserve respect and support. In this fight of our tribal brothers and sisters, the Congress and I stand with them,” he had written on X, sharing a video from the meeting.
During the meeting, protestors claimed that the KBLP would impact around 7,000 families in 21 tribal-dominated villages in the two districts as well as about 46 lakh trees as part of the project falls under the Panna Tiger Reserve.

briefs.headline: NEET is more than an exam. It is a social contract
briefs.deck: NEET is more than an exam. It is a social contract
briefs.bodyText: The constitution of the high-powered task force on examination reforms, led by Nandan Nilekani, comes at a time when public confidence in India’s examination system has been badly shaken. India has an opportunity to do something much larger than fix an examination. The immediate questions are familiar: paper leaks, examination security, technology, logistics, impersonation, and whether NEET should move from pen-and-paper to a computer-based format. All these questions matter. But they are not the most important. The Nilekani task force must examine something more fundamental: What should a national examination be designed to do?.NEET is not simply an examination. For millions of young Indians, it is a social contract. A student who spends two or three years preparing for NEET is not merely preparing to answer questions. Behind that preparation are parents who have saved, borrowed or sacrificed; teachers who have invested time; children who have postponed other choices; and families that see medicine as a pathway to social mobility. For many first-generation aspirants, NEET represents the possibility that merit can overcome privilege. That is why a compromised examination does such extraordinary damage. What is lost is not merely a few marks. The connection between effort and reward is broken. Therefore, NEET reform must begin with the restoration of trust..After the protests | Restore trust in public examinations.The first principle of reform should be trust by design. Every stage – from question paper creation to delivery, testing, scoring, and admissions – should be auditable. Every stakeholder should know where accountability lies. Candidates should have predictable rules for disruption, technical failure, grievance redress, and re-testing. The system should be designed so that no single failure can destroy an entire cohort’s future..However, a second question deserves much greater attention: Does a federal country need one common examination for every institution? India is a Union of states. Education is in the concurrent list. Medical education requires national standards, but the institutions that educate our doctors belong to very different governance structures: central institutions, state institutions, private colleges, and deemed universities. Yet we have gradually constructed an architecture in which one national examination has become the gateway to almost all undergraduate medical education..Uniformity has obvious advantages. It creates a common benchmark, reduces the scope for arbitrary institutional selection, facilitates national mobility, and can curb some of the opacity and malpractice that historically accompanied multiple entrance examinations. But uniformity and centralisation are not the same thing. India could consider a different architecture: a National Examination Architecture, rather than a National Examination Monopoly..The Government of India could conduct a national common entrance examination for central institutions and for institutions whose admissions are appropriately organised at the national level, including participating deemed universities. States, meanwhile, could have the option – subject to clearly defined national guardrails – to conduct their own common entrance examinations for government and private medical colleges within the state..The principle would be simple: Common standards and multiple trusted pathways. The Union would prescribe the guardrails: curriculum and competency standards, examination-security protocols, question-setting norms, psychometric standards, statistical equating where necessary, cybersecurity requirements, auditability, grievance redress, and penalties for malpractice. A state examination that meets those standards ought to be recognised as a valid pathway into the state’s medical institutions. This would not weaken national standards. It could strengthen them..There is also a federal principle at stake. States should not be reduced to mere implementing agencies for a national education policy. They should have the institutional capacity to innovate, experiment, and take responsibility for outcomes within their jurisdiction. A state that believes it can administer a more trusted, equitable or context-sensitive examination should have the opportunity to demonstrate that capability..The third principle should be to reduce the consequences of a single day. It is astonishing that the future of millions of young people can depend upon their performance during a few hours on one particular day. The system should explore multiple testing windows, calibrated question banks, and robust statistical equating, allowing more than one opportunity without compromising comparability..Finally, reform must ask whether we are testing what we actually value. If medicine requires reasoning, scientific understanding, interpretation, judgement, and the ability to apply knowledge to unfamiliar situations, then our assessment system should reward these capabilities rather than disproportionately rewarding memorisation under extreme time pressure. This matters even more in the age of artificial intelligence. AI is making information retrieval progressively cheaper. The value of human capability lies increasingly in reasoning, judgement, empathy, and the application of knowledge. Our examinations should begin preparing for that future..The challenge is to make India’s examination architecture harder to distrust. The real question is whether young Indians can believe that effort, merit, and integrity still have a place in the republic..The writer is the former civil servant enjoys traversing the myriad spaces of ideas, thinkers, and books.Disclaimer: The views expressed above are the author's own. briefs.deck: Sirwar gang-rape & murder: 4 cops suspended for dereliction of duty

stories.headline: Park Bill: Move aimed at facilitating takeover of Lalbagh land for Tunnel Road, say environmentalists, city BJP MPs
stories.deck: The Karnataka Cabinet on Friday cleared a Bill to amend the Karnataka Government Parks (Preservation) Act, 1975, to allow 5% of parks and garden lands to be alienated for public purposes
stories.bodyText:
The Karnataka Cabinet clearing a Bill to amend the Karnataka Government Parks (Preservation) Act, 1975, to allow 5% of parks and garden lands to be alienated for public purposes, drew severe criticism from citizen groups, environmentalists, and BJP MPs from the city.
Reading the Amendment in the context of recent developments, environmentalists and citizens have alleged that the move is aimed at facilitating the 17.1-km Bengaluru North-South Twin Tunnel Road, which starts at Hebbal and ends at Central Silk Board Junction.
‘To defend case’
Dattatreya T. Devare, an environmental activist, said that laws were now being amended to defend the case against the tunnel project in the High Court of Karnataka, which is hearing a batch of three public interest litigations challenging the project.
“The petitioners have raised objections to the Tunnel Road project based on a review of the ambit of the existing laws, including the Karnataka Government Parks (Preservation) Act, 1975. Now this law is being amended. This move is purely to escape from the petitions against both the long and short tunnels,” Mr. Devare told The Hindu.
The Amendment is intended to accommodate the “sacrosanct projects” and could defeat whatever points the petitioners have raised, he said. He expressed concern that any opposition to the proposed projects is either being ignored or defeated through amendments, citing the recent reduction of buffer zones along drains to accommodate roads along the buffer zones.
The court, on July 16, directed the government that the fate of the Tunnel Road project would be dependent on the outcome of the court case.
BJP MPs oppose
L.S. Tejasvi Surya, Bengaluru South BJP MP, took to social media and said the Tunnel Project would pass through Lalbagh and require around 1.92 hectares (nearly five acres) for the tunnel and shaft. The Detailed Project Report also proposes parking and a commercial complex around the shaft, he said.
“This move is clearly designed to facilitate projects such as the Tunnel Road by circumventing the proceedings before the Honourable High Court,” he said. In an open letter to Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar on Saturday, Mr. Surya said the State Cabinet’s decision could have serious implications for the city’s remaining green spaces.
P.C. Mohan, Bengaluru Central BJP MP, termed the Bill “a dangerous assault on Bengaluru’s green spaces.” “Laws protecting Lalbagh and Cubbon Park must be strengthened, not diluted to enable projects,” he said, announcing that the BJP will oppose this Bill.
It is not yet clear whether the Bill will be tabled in the ongoing Karnataka Legislature Session.

stories.headline: West Bengal Muslims say they are caught in crackdown on Bangladeshis
stories.deck: Many migrants labourers from West Bengal claim they are being repeatedly detained and harassed by the police in Bengaluru
stories.bodyText:
After being repeatedly detained, allegedly beaten up by the police because they believe he was an illegal Bangladeshi immigrant, Murshida’s husband left the family behind and returned to his native state West Bengal four months ago. “Why should we run like this when we are Indians? What have we done to receive this treatment?” asked Murshida.
Murshida is one among many migrants from West Bengal who say they are being repeatedly detained and harassed by the police in Bengaluru.
“When he said he would leave, my seven-year-old daughter started crying, so he took her too. I have not seen my husband or daughter for months,” she said, showing a copy of the enumeration form her husband recently filled during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) in Karnataka. “The form indicates he is a citizen here.”
“He got the enumeration form here in Bengaluru as he has been voting here for years, while my voter ID is in Basanti town of South 24 Parganas district. Many people were scaring us that he would not get the form here because he was not a citizen. When he got the form, he immediately called home and asked for his parents’ 2002 details, filled it up and submitted it.” But even that has now become another source of fear for the family. His name and other details do not match across his documents, and he fears that these discrepancies could once again subject him to police harassment.
Ready with documents
Pointing to the thick file of photocopies, Murshida said, “We keep copies ready whenever they detain us. But why this treatment? What have we done?”
Murshida has been living in Bengaluru with her husband and other members of the family since 2008. She first worked as a domestic help in an apartment in Electronics City and later as a cook. Last year, after she became pregnant again, she stopped working and began relying on her husband. Now, he too has left.
“He does video calls and shows my daughter, but he is in constant fear. I request him each day to come back but he says he cannot take this kind of treatment anymore,” Murshida said.
She said the ordeal began around Eid this year, when the family returned to Bengaluru after celebrating the festival in West Bengal. Someone told the police that “Bangladeshis in large number are coming in the train” and shared a clip of migrants arriving at Majestic railway station. “After that, the police detained us and released only a few days later,” she said.
Not alone
For Mohammed Sheikh and Ameen, the story has turned even more bitter. Until last year, they used to accompany the police during drives to identify “Bangladeshis” and are now themselves termed as Bangladeshis.
“We can identify from the accent and the words who is originally from Bengal and who is not. We knew where these people lived and would be their informants. And now we are being made ‘Bangladeshi’ by the Bangladeshis themselves,” claimed Mohammed Sheikh, who works as a scrap collector in Bhoopasandra.
Mohammed added, “Police know where the Bangladeshis are, but we are their easy targets. They take us, beat us and, in many cases, leave us in the middle of the city. We find it difficult to return to where we live because we neither know the language nor know our way around the city. We do not even go around alone and mostly remain in groups at our places of work,” he said, recalling one instance when he was beaten up and left at Shantinagar.
While Mohammed is a migrant from West Bengal, Ameen, 43, was born and brought up in Bengaluru. His family has been living in Chikkaballapur for generations.
Months ago, Ameen said, he filed a petition with the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) as well as the city police, giving them details of where Bangladeshi migrants live. Ever since then, instead of acting on the information, he said, the police began questioning him about how he knew them and whether he had links with them.
Police deny allegations
However, rejecting claims of harassment, Bengaluru City Police Commissioner Seemant Kumar Singh said that all arrests were made based on information received and that there was no question of wrongly framing or questioning a genuine Indian citizen.

stories.headline: I want to bring back Kuchipudi’s dance-drama style to Karnataka: Veena Murthy Vijay
stories.deck: 50 years on, Veena Murthy Vijay wants to bring the old dance-drama style back to Karnataka after winning the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award for Kuchipudi
stories.bodyText:
For Dr Veena Murthy Vijay, the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award for Kuchipudi is both a recognition of the past and a push towards the future. President Droupadi Murmu conferred the award for the year 2024 on her at Vigyan Bhawan in New Delhi on August 13. The honour comes as Murthy Vijay’s Bengaluru-based school, founded in 1976, marks its 50th year.
In a conversation with 
Bangalore Times
, the veteran dancer, choreographer and teacher reflects on five decades of her journey in Karnataka, reviving Kuchipudi’s dance-drama tradition, and why dance still matters to young people in an age of Instagram and Netflix.
Dance is not all about a drill or a body exercise. It is about the mind, emotions, and looking into your own self. The journey shapes your personality
Veena Murthy Vijay
Shedding light on the next chapter, Murthy Vijay says she wishes to take Kuchipudi deeper into Karnataka and revive its original dance-drama format rather than limiting it to the solo repertoire that audiences largely see today. “I want to bring more Kuchipudi into Karnataka. I want to bring back that dance-drama style and the original Yakshagana style here,” she says. She also hopes more students will take up certificate and diploma courses that explore the theatrical aspects of Kuchipudi.
At the same time, she believes the art form must leave room for experimentation, especially when it comes to younger dancers. “When you experiment with something, it is like cooking something new. 
Sometimes you fail, sometimes you are successful. Change is the one constant we must see,” she says.
But experimentation, she stresses, should not come at the cost of tradition. “That doesn’t mean that you ignore the traditional pedagogy. Based on these principles, any improvement or enhancement is most welcome.”
I want to bring more Kuchipudi into Karnataka. I want to bring back that dance-drama style and the original Yakshagana style here
Veena Murthy Vijay
After watching generations of students take to the arts, Murthy Vijay believes dance can offer children far more than physical training or performance skills. “Dance is not all about a drill or a body exercise. It is about the mind, emotions, and looking into your own self. The journey shapes your personality,” she says. For her, the motivation to remain immersed in dance has never been fame or money. “I feel there is a purpose to my life when I think about dance. That is what has made me and driven me,” she shares.
And perhaps that is what the award means most to her — an opportunity to give back to the art that has shaped her life. “I want to see many youngsters dancing. It makes me very, very happy when I see youngsters following their passion instead of watching Instagram and Netflix,” she adds.

stories.headline: 58km Blue Line Metro to Bengaluru airport will be operational in two years: Minister
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Namma Metro’s much-awaited Blue Line, connecting Central Silk Board with Kempegowda International Airport (KIA), is now expected to be fully operational by March 2028, with the 58km corridor set to open in phases, Bengaluru development minister Krishna Byre Gowda said Saturday.
The new deadline marks a three-month delay from BMRCL’s earlier target of commissioning the entire line by Dec 2027. Challenges in constructing a four-track Metro viaduct between Hebbal and Kempapura, to facilitate integration with the proposed Orange Line, are among the reasons behind the revised schedule, officials said.
The minister, who inspected the underground section of Pink Line between MG Road and Shivajinagar, said BMRCL has drawn up a plan to commission Blue Line in three stages.
He said works on the Central Silk Board–KR Pura stretch are at an advanced stage. Trial runs on KR Pura–Iblur section are expected to begin by Oct, while those between Iblur and Central Silk Board are scheduled for Dec 2026. “Commercial operations on Central Silk Board–KR Pura corridor are expected to start by mid-2027,” Gowda said.
The Hebbal–KIA section is targeted for opening by Sept 2027. The remaining KR Pura–Hebbal section, including the stretch through Nagawara, is expected to be completed between Dec 2027 and March 2028.
According to the minister, Metro construction between Hebbal and Nagawara is facing multiple execution challenges. Building stations and viaducts along the traffic-heavy Outer Ring Road (ORR) corridor has proved to be particularly difficult. Another major challenge is integrating Blue Line with the proposed Orange Line between JP Nagar and Kempapura.
“As part of the integration plan, BMRCL is constructing an elevated corridor capable of accommodating four tracks between Hebbal and Kempapura. Instead of returning to carry out major construction works when Orange Line is commissioned several years later, we are building the infrastructure for four tracks now itself,” the minister explained.
A senior BMRCL official said a specialised three-pier portal structure is being constructed along the 1km stretch between Hebbal and Kempapura to accommodate four Metro tracks. This will be the first such four-track elevated configuration on Namma Metro’s mainline network.
Pink Line elevated stretch likely in Sept
BMRCL is preparing to open the first section of the 21km Pink Line by Sept. The 7.5km elevated stretch between Kalena Agrahara and Tavarekere was earlier expected to open in Aug. Currently, BMRCL is awaiting certification from railways for its rolling stock.
Gowda said the inauguration will depend on the availability of the chief minister and the central govt.
However, substantial work remains to be done on the 13km underground section between Dairy Circle and Nagawara. The section was earlier targeted for opening by March 2027. Gowda said he has directed BMRCL officials to speed up system works and begin trial runs from Jayadeva side.
Pink Line, connecting Kalena Agrahara and Nagawara through key areas such as MG Road and Shivajinagar, will provide a crucial north-south link through Bengaluru’s central business district. Its interchange with the Blue Line at Nagawara will eventually offer Metro connectivity towards KIA via Hebbal.
The minister said Rs 12,000 crore has been provided for Pink Line. “Despite various challenges, including the impact of Covid, the project has now reached an advanced stage,” Gowda said.
He refused to comment on Tamil Nadu govt’s proposal for an inter-state Metro link between Hosur and Bommasandra. On demands for Metro connectivity to Bengaluru’s satellite towns and neighbouring districts, he said Metro alone cannot address long-distance regional transport needs. “There is a need to integrate Metro with other modes such as Bengaluru suburban rail and regional rapid transit system. I have instructed officials to explore these possibilities,” the minister added.

briefs.headline: Number plate arrives after a year, Bengaluru consumer court orders firm to pay Rs 5,000
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 A simple online order for a High Security Registration Plate (HSRP) turned into a 16-month ordeal for a Yelahanka resident after the company repeatedly failed to deliver it despite numerous follow-ups and false assurances. He eventually approached Bangalore Urban II Additional District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, which directed the company to pay compensation and litigation costs.
The ordeal began on March 2, 2024, when 38-year-old Amogh GM ordered an HSRP plate through the company’s website, paying Rs 761 by credit card. He received a payment receipt and an appointment confirmation for fitment on March 18 at a designated dealer location. However, when he arrived at the location on the appointed date, the dealer told him the plate hadn’t been received and asked him to return after a week.
Over the following months, Amogh repeatedly contacted the fitment dealer, only to be told that the plate had not yet arrived. After waiting for three months, he approached Rosemerta Safety Systems Limited’s Magadi Road customer support on June 13, 2024. The company responded on June 15, saying the matter had been escalated. 
When he followed up again on June 28, he received a similar assurance the next day, but repeated calls and messages through July yielded no resolution.
On Aug 1, Amogh was informed by Rosemerta’s support team that the plate had been delivered to the dealer. However, when he contacted the dealer, Amogh was told it had exited the HSRP business and was directed back to Rosemerta. Seeking the delivery address on Sept 20, Amogh again received assurances from the company that the issue would be resolved, but no concrete solution followed.
On Nov 20, he pointed out that govt’s HSRP installation deadline had lapsed and that eight months had passed since his order. On Dec 2, an unidentified caller claimed the plate was ready but stopped responding after Amogh asked for it to be posted.
On Feb 20, 2025, he received a message saying the plate was at a dealer location and could be collected on March 28, but no address was provided. Despite further follow-ups, Amogh never received the plate.
Having lost patience after more than a year of delay and repeated false assurances, Amogh warned firm executives that he would issue a legal notice. Only then, on July 12, 2025, they delivered the number plate to him.
Amogh filed a consumer complaint on Sept 23. Despite notice, the firm neither appeared nor filed a reply and proceeded against ex parte.
After going through the documents, the commission bench of president Anuradha V and member Savitha Airani held that Rosemerta’s failure to deliver the product within time and making the complainant “run from pillar to post,” amounted to deficiency of service and unfair trade practice.
The commission ordered Rosemerta to pay Rs 3,000 towards mental agony and harassment and Rs 2,000 towards litigation costs.

briefs.headline: Expired drug bust in Karnataka: Doctors flag the danger beyond date
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 How dangerous can expired medicines be? The question has gained urgency after police recently busted a fake drug racket in Bidadi and seized expired medicines worth Rs 35 lakh from a farmhouse. While expired drugs do not necessarily turn toxic immediately after crossing their expiry date, doctors say loss of potency can lead to treatment failure, while certain high-alert medicines can cause serious harm if used after expiry.
“Expired drugs primarily lose their efficacy. But with high-alert medications used in CCUs and ICUs, chemotherapy drugs and certain cardiac medicines, administering them after expiry can potentially cause toxicity and harm to the patient,” said Dr Preema Khan, consultant — internal medicine, KIMS Hospitals, Electronics City.
She added that expired antibiotics were particularly concerning, as reduced effectiveness could result in treatment failure and potentially contribute to difficult-to-treat infections and drug resistance.
According to doctors, the consequences of taking an expired medicine depend on the drug, its formulation, storage conditions, dose, and the patient’s health. “An expired medicine does not necessarily become hazardous on the very day it crosses its expiry date. 
In most instances, the concern is it becomes less effective or ineffective because it loses potency over time. However, stability differs between medicines and also depends on how they have been stored,” said Dr Manohar KN, lead consultant – internal medicine and diabetology, SPARSH Hospital, Hennur Road.
Heat, humidity and sunlight can affect the chemical and physical stability of medicines, he added. Liquids, suspensions, and eye drops may be particularly vulnerable to degradation or contamination. Importantly, a medicine may appear normal even when its chemical stability has been compromised.
According to Dr Aravinda SN, lead consultant – internal medicine, Aster RV Hospital, heat can accelerate chemical breakdown, while humidity can affect tablets, capsules and powders. Certain light-sensitive medicines can also degrade when exposed to sunlight or UV light.
The risk is particularly significant for insulin, injectable drugs and hormones, where maintaining the recommended storage temperature is critical, doctors said.
Labels matter
The concerns become more serious when the medicine is spurious or incorrectly labelled. “The risk can be much higher because a spurious medicine might include the wrong ingredient, mismatched strength, contaminants, or even an active component that is missing entirely,” said Dr Aravinda.
The effects can range from nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dizziness and drowsiness to confusion, palpitations, changes in blood pressure and allergic reactions. Severe poisoning can cause seizures, breathing difficulties, altered consciousness and abnormal heart rhythms.
Dr Preema said hypersensitive patients could develop skin rashes and other allergic reactions, while severe cases could involve breathing difficulty, low blood pressure, hypoxia and even cardiac or respiratory arrest.
Doctors also cautioned that contaminated, incorrectly formulated, or excessively dosed medicines can cause organ damage, particularly to the liver and kidneys. “The liver metabolises a lot of medicines, while the kidneys help eliminate many drugs and their breakdown products. An unexpectedly high dose, toxic ingredient or medicine unsuitable for a particular patient can therefore increase the risk of organ injury,” said Dr Aravinda.
From minutes to days
Toxicity can occur within minutes or hours with some rapidly acting or overdosed medicines, while in other cases symptoms may take days to appear. Children, older adults, pregnant women and patients with kidney or liver disease may be particularly vulnerable to medication-related harm.
Doctors advised patients who suspect they have taken an expired, spurious or incorrectly labelled medicine not to wait for symptoms before seeking medical advice, particularly if the identity or dose is unclear. “They should also hang onto the medicine strip, bottle, packaging, batch number and expiry details... They should jot down roughly how much was consumed and when it happened. Don’t induce vomiting or take another medicine ‘just in case’ unless a healthcare professional tells you to,” said Dr Aravinda.
Medical experts said treatment failure may sometimes be the first indication that a medicine has not worked as expected, rather than an obvious toxic reaction. Dr Preema also stressed the need for healthcare providers to strengthen systems for tracking expired and near-expiry medicines to prevent expired products from being administered or relabelled.

briefs.headline: ‘Missing’ Karnataka IAS officer is in hometown: Minister
briefs.bodyText:

 Home minister Priyank Kharge Saturday said IAS officer Gyanendra Kumar, believed to have gone incommunicado for the past few days, had sought leave due to a family emergency and had travelled to his hometown. Karnataka
 Public Service Commission (
